rationale: A wins because it keeps the caveats in the story instead of decorating around them. Its line, "The study is the story, limits included," is exactly the discipline this update needs. B has real instincts, but "Are health insurers using a meditation app instead of paying for real anxiety care?" jumps from a covered app benefit to a substitution/parity fight the facts do not prove. That is how a useful skeptical angle becomes a lawsuit-shaped pothole.
gaps_in_A: "Its next 25 million users won't pay it directly" overstates the fact. The update says 25 million eligible insurance members, not 25 million users.
"category-creation" is a little grand. Three insurers covering Calm is a strong coverage-line story, but not automatically proof a new category has been created.
A does not fully surface the harder policy-access question: whether this app benefit complements clinical mental-health care or gives insurers a cheaper story to tell.
gaps_in_B: "Insurers just made Calm a default benefit for 25 million Americans" invents both "default" and "Americans." The update says covered benefit for estimated members, with no geography supplied.

"Are health insurers using a meditation app instead of paying for real anxiety care?" is a loaded accusation the facts do not support. It needs evidence of substitution, not just a provocative question mark.
"employer and payer mental-health benefit design" drags employers into an insurer deal without support from the update.
B misses the member-engagement angle hiding in plain sight: the 18% anxiety reduction was among "regular users," while the 25 million figure is eligibility, not usage.
